pos: n. (a body of inland water; in Luke, the sea of Galilee; in Revelation, the lake of fire)
etymology: Latin lacus, a basin or pool. Only two lakes appear in the Authorized Version: Gennesaret, where our Lord taught from a boat, and the lake of fire, which is the last thing named before the new heaven and the new earth.
biblical_def: Luke, alone among the evangelists, calls the sea of Galilee a lake — the accurate word for a body of fresh water thirteen miles long. He stood by “the lake of Gennesaret” and taught out of Simon's ship because the people pressed upon Him (Luk 5:1-2). He crossed it asleep, and “there came down a storm of wind on the lake; and they were filled with water, and were in jeopardy” (Luk 8:23). And on the far shore the devils entered the swine and “the herd ran violently down a steep place into the lake, and were choked” (Luk 8:33). The other lake is named five times in Revelation and is the final destination of everything that opposed God. The beast and the false prophet are “cast alive into a lake of fire burning with brimstone” (Rev 19:20); then the devil (Rev 20:10); then, remarkably, “death and hell were cast into the lake of fire. This is the second death” (Rev 20:14) — death itself destroyed by being thrown into it. And then the persons: “whosoever was not found written in the book of life was cast into the lake of fire” (Rev 20:15). Scripture's two lakes are a Galilean fishing water where the Saviour slept in a storm, and the everlasting fire He came to save men from.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines lake as a large and extensive collection of water contained in a cavity or hollow of the earth; and notes that lakes are usually fresh water.
webster_full: LAKE, n. A large and extensive collection of water contained in a cavity or hollow of the earth.
1. It is used in Scripture for the sea of Galilee, or lake of Gennesaret.
BRIMSTONE, n. Sulphur; a hard, brittle, inflammable substance, of a lemon yellow color.
SECOND DEATH, in Scripture, the final and everlasting punishment of the wicked.
scriptures: And death and hell were cast into the lake of fire. This is the second death.
And whosoever was not found written in the book of life was cast into the lake of fire.
Luk 5:1
And it came to pass, that, as the people pressed upon him to hear the word of God, he stood by the lake of Gennesaret,
Luk 8:23
But as they sailed he fell asleep: and there came down a storm of wind on the lake; and they were filled with water, and were in jeopardy.
corruption_summary: The lake of fire is reinterpreted as annihilation or as a symbol of eventual restoration; Revelation says tormented day and night for ever and ever.
corruption_paragraphs: Two departures from the historic doctrine attach to these verses. Annihilationism holds that the lost are destroyed rather than punished consciously without end, and universalism holds that the fire purges and all are finally restored. Revelation 20:10 answers both in one clause: the devil, the beast and the false prophet shall be tormented day and night for ever and ever — the same phrase used elsewhere in the book of the worship of God, so that if the one is unending the other is. Our Lord Himself, who spoke of hell more than anyone in Scripture, used the identical adjective for both destinies in a single sentence: these shall go away into everlasting punishment: but the righteous into life eternal.

This doctrine is not to be preached with any relish, and a man who can announce it without grief has misunderstood it. But it may not be quietly dropped either, because the whole weight of the gospel rests on what is actually at stake. Revelation 20:15 gives the one distinction that matters — whosoever was not found written in the book of life — and the book of life belongs to the Lamb that was slain. The right response to the lake of fire is the one Jude gives: and others save with fear, pulling them out of the fire.
roots_summary: Greek limne (G3041), a lake; limne tou puros, the lake of fire; theion (G2303), brimstone, sulphur.
roots_lines: Greek limne (G3041) — a lake; Luke 5:1-2, 8:22-33 of Gennesaret, and Revelation 19:20, 20:10-15, 21:8 of the lake of fire.
Greek Gennesaret (G1082) — the plain and lake on the western shore of the sea of Galilee.
Greek theion (G2303) — brimstone, sulphur; burning with fire and brimstone, the imagery of Sodom carried to the last judgment.
Greek basanizo (G928) — to torment, to test by touchstone; Revelation 20:10, tormented day and night.
Greek biblos tes zoes (G976, G2222) — the book of life; Revelation 20:15, 21:27, the register that decides the case.
usage: “Death and hell were cast into the lake of fire” — death itself destroyed.
“He stood by the lake of Gennesaret” — and taught from a fisherman's boat.
“There came down a storm of wind on the lake” — and He was asleep.

pos: n. (the central stem of the golden candlestick; and an arrow)
etymology: Saxon sceaft, a rod or pole. The Authorized Version uses it for two things only, and both are worth holding together: the central stem from which the lamps of the sanctuary branched, and the polished arrow hidden in God's quiver.
biblical_def: “Thou shalt make a candlestick of pure gold: of beaten work shall the candlestick be made: his shaft, and his branches, his bowls, his knops, and his flowers, shall be of the same” (Exo 25:31). The shaft is the central stem, and the whole lampstand — stem, six branches, almond bowls, knops and flowers — was hammered out of a single talent of gold, “according unto the pattern which the LORD had shewed Moses” (Num 8:4). One piece, beaten, not assembled: the branches are not attached to the shaft, they are the shaft, drawn out of it. That is the picture our Lord takes up in John 15 — I am the vine, ye are the branches — and John sees seven candlesticks in Revelation 1 with the Son of man walking in their midst. The other shaft is an arrow, in the second Servant song: “he hath made my mouth like a sharp sword; in the shadow of his hand hath he hid me, and made me a polished shaft; in his quiver hath he hid me” (Isa 49:2). The Servant is a weapon prepared in secret — polished by long attention, kept hidden in the quiver, drawn at the appointed moment. Both hiddenness and readiness are God's work, and the preparation is the greater part of it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines shaft as an arrow, a missile weapon; the stem or stock of a thing; and the body of a column, between the base and the capital.
webster_full: SHAFT, n. An arrow; a missive weapon.
1. The stem, stock or body of any thing; as the shaft of a column.
2. In architecture, the shaft of a column is the body between the base and the capital.
3. A deep pit; a narrow opening into a mine.
QUIVER, n. A case or sheath for arrows.
scriptures: And thou shalt make a candlestick of pure gold: of beaten work shall the candlestick be made: his shaft, and his branches, his bowls, his knops, and his flowers, shall be of the same.
Isa 49:2
And he hath made my mouth like a sharp sword; in the shadow of his hand hath he hid me, and made me a polished shaft; in his quiver hath he hid me;
Num 8:4

And this work of the candlestick was of beaten gold, unto the shaft thereof, unto the flowers thereof, was beaten work: according unto the pattern which the LORD had shewed Moses, so he made the candlestick.
And he made the candlestick of pure gold: of beaten work made he the candlestick; his shaft, and his branch, his bowls, his knops, and his flowers, were of the same:
corruption_summary: Visible usefulness is treated as the measure of a servant; Isaiah 49 says God polishes His arrow and then hides it in the quiver.
corruption_paragraphs: In his quiver hath he hid me is a sentence the modern church has almost no category for. Everything in our formation is arranged toward visibility — platform, output, measurable ministry — and the Servant of Isaiah 49 is described as polished and then hidden, kept in the shadow of God's hand until the moment of drawing. Moses had forty years in Midian, Paul had years in Arabia and Tarsus, and our Lord Himself had thirty in a carpenter's shop. The polishing is the work and the quiver is the place; a man who cannot bear being hidden is not yet finished being made.

The candlestick supplies the companion truth about the church. Shaft and branches were one beaten piece, hammered from a single talent of gold according to a pattern shewed on the mount. Nothing was assembled and nothing was improvised. The branches had no independent existence, no light of their own, and no way of being a lamp apart from the stem they were drawn out of. Every doctrine of the church as a voluntary association of individuals who have decided to cooperate founders on that lampstand, and on the vine our Lord compared Himself to: without me ye can do nothing.
roots_summary: Hebrew yarek (H3409), the thigh, the shaft or base of the candlestick; chets (H2671), an arrow; barur (H1305), polished, purified.
roots_lines: Hebrew yarek (H3409) — thigh, side, base; Exodus 25:31, 37:17, Numbers 8:4, the central shaft of the candlestick.
Hebrew miqshah (H4749) — beaten work, hammered out of one piece; the required method for the lampstand.
Hebrew chets (H2671) — an arrow; Isaiah 49:2, a polished shaft.
Hebrew barur (H1305) — polished, purified, choice; the participle describing the arrow's preparation.
Hebrew 'ashpah (H827) — a quiver; where the arrow is hidden until it is drawn.
usage: “His shaft, and his branches… shall be of the same” — one beaten piece.
“Made me a polished shaft; in his quiver hath he hid me”.
“According unto the pattern which the LORD had shewed Moses”.

pos: n. (in the Authorized Version, hardened metal — usually rendering the Hebrew for brass or bronze in the phrase a bow of steel)
etymology: Saxon stael. The translators used steel for the Hebrew nechushah, burnished bronze, in the phrase a bow of steel — a bow of the hardest metal known, and therefore the standing image of a strength no man can bend.
biblical_def: David's song, recorded twice, contains the boast: “He teacheth my hands to war, so that a bow of steel is broken by mine arms” (Psa 18:34; 2Sa 22:35). The bow of hardest metal is the hardest thing a man could be asked to bend, and David does not say that he is strong; he says that He teacheth my hands. The whole psalm is built on that grammar — God is the rock, the fortress, the deliverer, the shield, the horn of salvation, and the strength for the impossible bow is His teaching. Zophar turns the same image into judgment on the wicked man: “He shall flee from the iron weapon, and the bow of steel shall strike him through” (Job 20:24) — escape the sword and the arrow finds you. And Jeremiah asks a question no one answers: “Shall iron break the northern iron and the steel?” (Jer 15:12). The northern iron is Babylon, and Judah's ordinary iron will not break it. The prophet who had just been told that his own strength would be as a defenced brasen wall (Jer 15:20) is shown that against Babylon the nation had none. Hardness in Scripture is a real quality of metal and a real quality of hearts, and only God bends either.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines steel as iron combined with carbon, harder and more elastic than iron; and figuratively, weapons, and extreme hardness of mind or heart.
webster_full: STEEL, n. Iron combined with a small portion of carbon; iron refined and hardened, used in making instruments.
1. Figuratively, weapons; particularly, offensive weapons, swords, spears and the like.
2. Extreme hardness; as heads or hearts of steel.
BRASS, n. An alloy of copper and zinc; in Scripture usually the Hebrew word for copper or bronze.
scriptures: He teacheth my hands to war, so that a bow of steel is broken by mine arms.
He teacheth my hands to war; so that a bow of steel is broken by mine arms.
He shall flee from the iron weapon, and the bow of steel shall strike him through.
Shall iron break the northern iron and the steel?
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The only point of confusion is metallurgical: the Hebrew word rendered steel is the ordinary word for burnished bronze, and the translators reached for the hardest metal their readers knew.

The principle to recover is the grammar of Psalm 18. David is describing genuine feats — running through a troop, leaping over a wall, bending a bow of bronze — and every one of them is credited to God in the same sentence: he teacheth my hands to war, thou hast girded me with strength, thy right hand hath holden me up, and, most tenderly, thy gentleness hath made me great. Scripture is not embarrassed by a man's real strength or skill; it simply refuses to let him keep the credit. That is the pattern for every ability a believer has: use it fully, and name its source honestly.
roots_summary: Hebrew nechushah (H5154), burnished bronze, copper — rendered steel; barzel (H1270), iron; qesheth (H7198), a bow.
roots_lines: Hebrew nechushah (H5154) — bronze, burnished copper; 2 Samuel 22:35, Job 20:24, Psalm 18:34, Jeremiah 15:12 — rendered steel in each.
Hebrew barzel (H1270) — iron; Jeremiah 15:12, shall iron break the northern iron?
Hebrew qesheth (H7198) — a bow; the bow of bronze no ordinary arm could bend.
Hebrew lamad (H3925) — to teach, to train; Psalm 18:34, he teacheth my hands to war.
Hebrew 'anvah (H6038) — gentleness, condescension; Psalm 18:35, thy gentleness hath made me great.
usage: “A bow of steel is broken by mine arms” — and He teacheth the hands.
“He shall flee from the iron weapon, and the bow of steel shall strike him through”.
“Shall iron break the northern iron and the steel?” — no answer is given.

pos: n. (a snare; a device hidden to catch a living thing)
etymology: Saxon treppe. A trap differs from a net in being hidden and in being sprung by the victim's own movement — which is exactly how Scripture uses it, of tables, of ways, and of men who set them for other men.
biblical_def: “Let their table become a snare before them: and that which should have been for their welfare, let it become a trap” (Psa 69:22). The imprecation is not that the wicked lose their table but that the very thing they trusted for good should turn on them. Paul quotes it in Romans 11:9 and applies it to Israel's hardening: “Let their table be made a snare, and a trap, and a stumblingblock, and a recompence unto them” — the covenant privileges themselves, the law, the temple, the descent from Abraham, became the ground of a self-confidence that shut them out of the righteousness of faith. Blessings held apart from Christ turn into snares; that is the doctrine, and it is aimed as much at churches with a great heritage as at Israel. Jeremiah shows the human traps: “among my people are found wicked men: they lay wait, as he that setteth snares; they set a trap, they catch men” (Jer 5:26) — a fowler's language for men who prey on their neighbours, and the phrase they catch men is a dark echo of our Lord's promise to make fishers of men. And Bildad, describing the fate of the wicked: “The snare is laid for him in the ground, and a trap for him in the way” (Job 18:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines trap as an engine that shuts suddenly, used for taking game; and figuratively, an ambush, a stratagem, any thing by which one is caught unawares.
webster_full: TRAP, n. An engine that shuts suddenly or with a spring, used for taking game.
1. An ambush; a stratagem; any device by which one is caught unawares.
TRAP, v.t. To catch in a trap; to insnare.
SNARE, n. An instrument for catching animals, particularly fowls, by the leg; anything by which one is entangled and brought into trouble.
scriptures: Let their table become a snare before them: and that which should have been for their welfare, let it become a trap.
Rom 11:9
And David saith, Let their table be made a snare, and a trap, and a stumblingblock, and a recompence unto them:
Jer 5:26
For among my people are found wicked men: they lay wait, as he that setteth snares; they set a trap, they catch men.
The snare is laid for him in the ground, and a trap for him in the way.
corruption_summary: Inherited religious privilege is treated as security; Paul says the table itself became the trap.
corruption_paragraphs: Romans 11:9 is one of the most uncomfortable applications in Scripture, and it is aimed at the most privileged people in the world — those to whom pertain the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the service of God and the promises. The table that should have been for their welfare became a trap. The mechanism is not that the gifts were bad but that they were made the ground of confidence apart from the righteousness of God: they being ignorant of God's righteousness, and going about to establish their own righteousness, have not submitted themselves unto the righteousness of God (Rom 10:3). Every church with a great confession, a faithful history and a sound heritage should read that sentence slowly.

The passage also forbids the opposite error, and Paul spends the whole chapter on it. Gentile believers are told plainly not to boast against the branches — thou standest by faith. Be not highminded, but fear — because the God who did not spare the natural branches will not spare the grafted ones on any different terms. The trap and the graft are the same doctrine seen from two sides: no man stands on his privileges, and every man stands by faith alone.
roots_summary: Hebrew moqesh (H4170), a bait, a lure, a snare; pach (H6341), a bird-trap, a snare; Greek thera (G2339), a hunting, a prey, a trap.
roots_lines: Hebrew moqesh (H4170) — a bait or lure, the striker of a trap; Psalm 69:22, Job 18:10 — the word also used of idols as a snare to Israel.
Hebrew pach (H6341) — a bird-trap, a snare of the fowler; Psalm 91:3, 124:7.
Hebrew yaqush (H3353) — a fowler, one who sets snares; Jeremiah 5:26, as he that setteth snares.
Greek thera (G2339) — a hunting, a catching, a prey; Romans 11:9, rendered trap.
Greek skandalon (G4625) — the trigger-stick of a trap, a stumblingblock; the third word in Paul's chain.
usage: “That which should have been for their welfare, let it become a trap”.
“Let their table be made a snare, and a trap” — the privileges themselves.
“They set a trap, they catch men” — among God's own people.

pos: v. (to frighten away; to scare off — the older sense preserved in afraid)
etymology: From Old French effrayer, to frighten; the same root that gives afraid. In the Authorized Version fray always means to scare a thing away, and twice the horror is that nobody is left alive to do it.
biblical_def: The word's first two uses are among the bleakest sentences in Scripture, and the bleakness is in what is not happening. In the covenant curses of Deuteronomy: “thy carcase shall be meat unto all fowls of the air, and unto the beasts of the earth, and no man shall fray them away” (Deu 28:26). Jeremiah repeats it over Jerusalem: “the carcases of this people shall be meat for the fowls of the heaven, and for the beasts of the earth; and none shall fray them away” (Jer 7:33). To be unburied was a disgrace in the ancient world, and to have no one even to wave the birds off is the picture of a society emptied out — no mourners, no family, no survivors. That is what the curse means. Against it stands Zechariah's night vision, where the word turns and becomes hope. The prophet sees four horns that scattered Judah, “so that no man did lift up his head”, and then four carpenters: “these are come to fray them, to cast out the horns of the Gentiles, which lifted up their horn over the land of Judah to scatter it” (Zec 1:21). The scatterers are themselves frightened away. God raises craftsmen against horns, and the people who could not lift up their heads are the ones He is defending.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines fray as to fright, to terrify; and notes that in this sense it is nearly obsolete, being superseded by afraid and affray.
webster_full: FRAY, v.t. To fright; to terrify.
1. To rub; to fret, as cloth by wearing.
FRAY, n. A broil, quarrel or violent riot.
AFRAID, pp. Impressed with fear; fearful. It is followed by of.
scriptures: Zec 1:21

Then said I, What come these to do? And he spake, saying, These are the horns which have scattered Judah, so that no man did lift up his head: but these are come to fray them, to cast out the horns of the Gentiles, which lifted up their horn over the land of Judah to scatter it.
And thy carcase shall be meat unto all fowls of the air, and unto the beasts of the earth, and no man shall fray them away.
Jer 7:33
And the carcases of this people shall be meat for the fowls of the heaven, and for the beasts of the earth; and none shall fray them away.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The verb has simply fallen out of use in this sense; a modern reader meets fray and thinks of a quarrel or of a worn edge, and misses that Deuteronomy 28:26 is describing carrion birds nobody drives off.

The principle to recover is that God raises instruments against the instruments of judgment. Zechariah 1 shows the prophet four horns — the powers that had gored and scattered Judah until no man could lift up his head — and then, without explanation, four carpenters, whose whole business is to fray the horns away. The vision is given to a discouraged remnant working on a half-built temple. It says that the same God who permitted the scattering has already appointed the men who will end it, and that He does it with craftsmen rather than with horns of His own. What frightens the powers of the earth is not a bigger horn but a workman sent by God.
roots_summary: Hebrew charad (H2729), to tremble, and causatively to make afraid; qeren (H7161), a horn; charash (H2796), a craftsman, a carpenter.
roots_lines: Hebrew charad (H2729) — to tremble, and in the causative to terrify, to drive away by frightening; Deuteronomy 28:26, Jeremiah 7:33, Zechariah 1:21.
Hebrew qeren (H7161) — a horn, the standing symbol of power; the four horns that scattered Judah.
Hebrew charash (H2796) — an engraver, craftsman, carpenter, smith; the four whom God raised against the horns.
Hebrew zarah (H2219) — to scatter, to winnow; what the horns had done to Judah.
Hebrew nebelah (H5038) — a carcase, a corpse; what the fowls were left undisturbed upon.
usage: “No man shall fray them away” — and that is the curse.
“None shall fray them away” — Jeremiah, over Jerusalem.
“These are come to fray them” — four carpenters against four horns.

pos: n. and adj. (an inlet of the sea — in Hebrew a tongue; a reddish-brown horse; and the bay tree)
etymology: Three unrelated words share the spelling. The geographic bay renders Hebrew lashon, a tongue of the sea; the bay horse is a reddish colour; and the bay tree is the laurel, an evergreen.
biblical_def: Joshua's land survey uses the word for the tongues of the Dead Sea: Judah's south border ran “from the shore of the salt sea, from the bay that looketh southward” (Jos 15:2), and the northern border “from the bay of the sea at the uttermost part of Jordan” (Jos 15:5); Benjamin's went out “at the north bay of the salt sea” (Jos 18:19). The Hebrew is lashon, a tongue — the sea putting out a tongue of water into the land. The most quoted use is the psalm's: “I have seen the wicked in great power, and spreading himself like a green bay tree” (Psa 37:35). The bay is the laurel, evergreen, never bare, with no visible season of decline — the perfect image of a prosperity that appears immune to time. The next verse finishes it: yet he passed away, and, lo, he was not: yea, I sought him, but he could not be found. The whole psalm is written to a believer fretting over the prosperity of the wicked, and its counsel is patience with a horizon. And Zechariah's fourth chariot has “grisled and bay horses” (Zec 6:3), which go forth to walk to and fro through the earth (Zec 6:7) — the four winds of heaven, standing before the Lord of all the earth, patrolling.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines bay as an arm of the sea extending into the land; as an adjective, red or reddish, inclining to a chestnut color, applied to horses; and the bay tree as the laurel.
webster_full: BAY, n. An arm of the sea, extending into the land, not of any definite form, but smaller than a gulf, and larger than a creek.
BAY, a. Red, or reddish, inclining to a chestnut color; applied to the color of horses.
BAY, n. The laurel tree; whence bays, an honorary garland or crown, bestowed as a prize for victory.
LAUREL, n. A tree of the genus Laurus; an evergreen.
scriptures: I have seen the wicked in great power, and spreading himself like a green bay tree.
Jos 15:2
And their south border was from the shore of the salt sea, from the bay that looketh southward:
Zec 6:3
And in the third chariot white horses; and in the fourth chariot grisled and bay horses.
And the border passed along to the side of Bethhoglah northward: and the outgoings of the border were at the north bay of the salt sea at the south end of Jordan: this was the south coast.
corruption_summary: The visible flourishing of the ungodly is taken as the last word; Psalm 37 grants the observation and moves the horizon.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 37 is written for a believer with a specific complaint: the wicked prosper, and it does not appear to matter what anyone does about it. The psalm never denies the observation — I have seen the wicked in great power, and spreading himself like a green bay tree — and the evergreen is exactly the right image, since a laurel has no bare season to give the game away. What the psalm does is extend the timeline: fret not thyself because of evildoers… for they shall soon be cut down like the grass, and then, one verse after the bay tree, he passed away, and, lo, he was not.

The pastoral instruction attached is worth naming, because it is not what most people would guess. The psalm does not tell the fretting believer to campaign, expose or avenge. It tells him to trust in the LORD, and do good; delight thyself also in the LORD; commit thy way unto him; rest in the LORD, and wait patiently for him. Envy of the prospering wicked is treated as a spiritual danger to the one who envies — fret not thyself in any wise to do evil — and the cure is occupation with God and with one's own duty.
roots_summary: Hebrew lashon (H3956), a tongue — a tongue of the sea, a bay; 'ezrach (H249), a native tree, rendered bay tree; 'amots (H554), strong or bay-coloured.
roots_lines: Hebrew lashon (H3956) — a tongue; Joshua 15:2, 15:5, 18:19 — the sea's tongue reaching into the land.
Hebrew 'ezrach (H249) — a native, one born in the land; Psalm 37:35, a tree native to its soil, rendered green bay tree.
Hebrew 'amots (H554) — strong, and by extension bay-coloured; Zechariah 6:3, 6:7, of the fourth chariot's horses.
Hebrew yam hammelach — the salt sea, the Dead Sea; the water these bays belong to.
Hebrew 'arits (H6184) — terrible, ruthless, a man of violence; Psalm 37:35, the wicked in great power.
usage: “Spreading himself like a green bay tree” — an evergreen has no bare season.
“From the bay that looketh southward” — a tongue of the salt sea.
“Grisled and bay horses” — the fourth chariot of the vision.

pos: adj. (pertaining to music; in the Authorized Version only in the phrase musical instruments)
etymology: From music, Greek mousike. The Authorized Version uses the adjective three times and always with instruments — twice of the instruments appointed for the worship of God, and once of the instruments a king gathered for his own delight.
biblical_def: Two of the three occurrences are liturgical and one is not, and the contrast is the entry. David set Heman and Jeduthun “with trumpets and cymbals for those that should make a sound, and with musical instruments of God” (1Ch 16:42) — instruments of God, appointed for His service, in the hands of appointed men, at the tabernacle he had pitched for the ark. At the dedication of the wall, Nehemiah's second company of singers went “with the musical instruments of David the man of God, and Ezra the scribe before them” (Neh 12:36). A century and a half after David, the instruments still bear his name and the pattern is deliberately resumed; reformation in Scripture consistently means returning to an appointed order rather than inventing a new one. The third use is Solomon's inventory of everything he tried: “I gat me men singers and women singers, and the delights of the sons of men, as musical instruments, and that of all sorts” (Ecc 2:8). The same art, and the whole passage ends all was vanity and vexation of spirit. Music offered to God in His appointed way, and music gathered to please oneself, are two different things done with the same strings.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines musical as belonging to music; and music as a succession of sounds so modulated as to please the ear, and in Scripture, the art employed in the worship of God.
webster_full: MUSICAL, a. Belonging to music; as musical proportion; a musical instrument.
1. Producing music or agreeable sounds; as a musical voice.
2. Melodious; harmonious; pleasing to the ear.
MUSIC, n. A succession of sounds so modulated as to please the ear, or a combination of simultaneous sounds in accordance or harmony.
scriptures: And with them Heman and Jeduthun with trumpets and cymbals for those that should make a sound, and with musical instruments of God. And the sons of Jeduthun were porters.
And his brethren, Shemaiah, and Azarael, Milalai, Gilalai, Maai, Nethaneel, and Judah, Hanani, with the musical instruments of David the man of God, and Ezra the scribe before them.
Ecc 2:8

I gathered me also silver and gold, and the peculiar treasure of kings and of the provinces: I gat me men singers and women singers, and the delights of the sons of men, as musical instruments, and that of all sorts.
corruption_summary: Corporate worship is arranged around what moves an audience; Scripture arranges it around what God has commanded.
corruption_paragraphs: The governing question in most modern worship planning is what will produce a response, and the tools are chosen accordingly — volume, lighting, arrangement, the emotional arc of a set. The regulative principle asks a different question first: what has God appointed for the worship of His people? What He has commanded is required, and what He has not commanded is not permitted in corporate worship. Under that rule the singing of the church is governed by the word, led by appointed men, and aimed at God rather than at the congregation's feelings. The Reformed have differed among themselves over instruments — some judging them part of the abrogated temple service and singing unaccompanied, others receiving them as a circumstance of worship — and that difference is held within the same principle, not against it.

Ecclesiastes 2:8 supplies the warning that no argument about instruments can settle. Solomon had the best musicians in the world, of all sorts, and lists them between his silver and his vineyards as part of an experiment in pleasing himself; and the verdict on the whole chapter is vanity. The same instrument may be an instrument of God in one man's hands and one of the delights of the sons of men in another's. What decides it is not the string but whether the worship was offered as He appointed and to Him.
roots_summary: Hebrew keli shir — instruments of song; keli ha'elohim — instruments of God; shirim (H7892), songs, singers.
roots_lines: Hebrew keli (H3627) — a vessel, an implement, an instrument; the same word used of the vessels of the sanctuary.
Hebrew keli shir — instruments of song; Nehemiah 12:36, 1 Chronicles 15:16.
Hebrew metsiltayim (H4700) — cymbals; 1 Chronicles 16:42, in the hands of the appointed Levites.
Hebrew Heman (H1968) and Yeduthun (H3038) — the two chief musicians David appointed, whose names head several psalms.
Greek psallo (G5567) — to pluck, to sing praise; Ephesians 5:19, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord.
usage: “With musical instruments of God” — appointed, and in appointed hands.
“The musical instruments of David the man of God” — resumed a century and a half later.
“As musical instruments, and that of all sorts” — and it was vanity.

pos: n. and pron. (one's own person; used in the Authorized Version chiefly in the emphatic mine own self, his own self, thine own self)
etymology: Saxon self. In the Authorized Version the bare noun almost always appears in an emphatic possessive phrase, and the two most important of those phrases belong to Christ — what He could not do of His own self, and what He bore in His own body.
biblical_def: The word's two great occurrences are both about the Son. First, His dependence: “I can of mine own self do nothing: as I hear, I judge: and my judgment is just; because I seek not mine own will, but the will of the Father which hath sent me” (Joh 5:30). The eternal Son, equal with the Father, says in His incarnate mission that He acts from no independent self-will. That is the pattern of every creature's proper relation to God, held perfectly by the only One who could have claimed otherwise. Second, His substitution: “Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree, that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness: by whose stripes ye were healed” (1Pe 2:24). Peter piles up the possessives — his own self, his own body — because the whole doctrine of the atonement stands on the personal, bodily, substitutionary bearing of sins that were not His. Then the same phrase in prayer, reaching back before creation: “glorify thou me with thine own self with the glory which I had with thee before the world was” (Joh 17:5). Paul uses it of judgment: “yea, I judge not mine own self” (1Co 4:3) — even his own verdict on himself is not final, for he that judgeth him is the Lord. And in Philemon, of a debt: Philemon owes Paul “even thine own self besides” (Phm 1:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines self as having its own or a single nature, as in self-love; and as expressing the individual person, in the emphatic forms myself, himself, thyself.
webster_full: SELF, pron. Having its own or a particular nature; united to a pronoun to express emphasis or distinction.
1. It is used to express the individual, as distinguished from all others.
2. In composition, self denotes something done by one's self, or of one's own nature; as self-denial, self-love, self-evident.
SELF-DENIAL, n. The denial of one's self; the forbearing to gratify one's own desires or appetites.
scriptures: Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree, that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness: by whose stripes ye were healed.
John 5:30
I can of mine own self do nothing: as I hear, I judge: and my judgment is just; because I seek not mine own will, but the will of the Father which hath sent me.
John 17:5
And now, O Father, glorify thou me with thine own self with the glory which I had with thee before the world was.
But with me it is a very small thing that I should be judged of you, or of man's judgment: yea, I judge not mine own self.
corruption_summary: The self has become the reference point of all value; Scripture makes it the thing to be denied and Christ the one who bore our sins in His own body.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern religion of the self — self-esteem as the root of health, self-actualization as the goal of life, self-expression as the highest honesty, the authentic self as the final authority — is a complete anthropology, and it is not the Bible's. Our Lord's terms are the exact reverse: if any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me. For whosoever will save his life shall lose it. This is not a call to self-hatred, which Scripture nowhere commands; the second great commandment assumes a man loves himself and tells him to love his neighbour that way. It is a call to dethrone the self as the reference point, which is a different thing entirely and a great deal harder.

The gospel's answer to the question of the self's worth is better than anything the self-esteem literature can offer, and it comes from outside. A man's value is not a verdict he passes on himself — Paul says even his own verdict does not count, I judge not mine own self — but the estimate of the One who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree. Nothing a person can say about himself, high or low, weighs against that transaction. And the freedom of it is enormous: a man who has stopped adjudicating his own worth can finally get on with loving his neighbour.
roots_summary: Greek autos (G846), self, the same, he himself; emautou (G1683), of myself; aparneomai (G533), to deny utterly — the verb of self-denial.
roots_lines: Greek autos (G846) — self, himself; 1 Peter 2:24, his own self — the emphatic pronoun carrying the personal substitution.
Greek emautou (G1683) — of myself, from my own initiative; John 5:30, I can of mine own self do nothing.
Greek soma (G4983) — body; 1 Peter 2:24, in his own body on the tree — the atonement is bodily.
Greek anaphero (G399) — to carry up, to bear up, as a sacrifice to an altar; the verb behind bare our sins.
Greek aparneomai (G533) — to deny utterly, to disown; Luke 9:23, let him deny himself — the same verb used of Peter denying Christ.
usage: “Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree”.
“I can of mine own self do nothing” — said by the Son.
“I judge not mine own self” — even Paul's verdict on Paul is not final.

pos: v. and n. (to survey, to look over; and the act of looking)
etymology: Old French veue, from Latin videre, to see. In the Authorized Version the verb is a scout's word — sent to view the land — and the noun is a watching place, where fifty men stood to see what would happen at the Jordan.
biblical_def: “Joshua the son of Nun sent out of Shittim two men to spy secretly, saying, Go view the land, even Jericho. And they went, and came into an harlot's house, named Rahab, and lodged there” (Jos 2:1). Two men, secretly, and the house they lodged in belonged to a Canaanite prostitute who hid them under stalks of flax, confessed that the LORD had given them the land, and asked for mercy — and she stands in Hebrews 11 among the heroes of faith and in Matthew 1 in the line of Christ. The second reconnaissance goes badly: “Joshua sent men from Jericho to Ai… Go up and view the country. And the men went up and viewed Ai” (Jos 7:2), and their report was that two or three thousand would do, and Israel fled before the men of Ai because of Achan's sin. The scouting was competent and the intelligence was worthless, because the problem was in the camp. And the noun: at the Jordan, “fifty men of the sons of the prophets went, and stood to view afar off: and they two stood by Jordan” (2Ki 2:7), and afterward “when the sons of the prophets which were to view at Jericho saw him, they said, The spirit of Elijah doth rest on Elisha” (2Ki 2:15). Fifty men watched from a distance what two men walked into.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines view as to survey, to examine with the eye, to inspect; and as a noun, the act of seeing, sight, prospect, or the power of seeing.
webster_full: VIEW, v.t. To survey; to examine with the eye; to look on with attention.
1. To see; to perceive by the eye.
2. To examine intellectually; to consider.
VIEW, n. Prospect; sight; reach of the eye.
1. The act of seeing or beholding; sight; survey.
scriptures: Jos 2:1
And Joshua the son of Nun sent out of Shittim two men to spy secretly, saying, Go view the land, even Jericho. And they went, and came into an harlot's house, named Rahab, and lodged there.
Jos 7:2
And Joshua sent men from Jericho to Ai, which is beside Bethaven, on the east side of Bethel, and spake unto them, saying, Go up and view the country. And the men went up and viewed Ai.
And fifty men of the sons of the prophets went, and stood to view afar off: and they two stood by Jordan.
And when the sons of the prophets which were to view at Jericho saw him, they said, The spirit of Elijah doth rest on Elisha.
corruption_summary: Failure is diagnosed as a failure of planning; Ai was scouted competently and lost because of a sin nobody had dealt with.
corruption_paragraphs: Joshua 7 is the standing rebuke to purely technical analysis. The reconnaissance of Ai was properly ordered and properly carried out; the men went up, viewed the country, and gave a professional assessment. The assessment was accurate about Ai and useless about Israel, because a man in the camp had taken of the accursed thing and God had said neither will I be with you any more, except ye destroy the accursed from among you. Churches and families in trouble reach for restructuring, better systems and better strategy with the same diligence and the same result. Some defeats are not intelligence problems. Joshua fell on his face and God told him to get up: Israel hath sinned.

The other half of the chapter is Rahab, and it must be preached alongside. The two spies who viewed Jericho found their whole mission resting on the confession of a Canaanite harlot, who said the LORD your God, he is God in heaven above, and in earth beneath, and asked for a token of mercy. She was saved with her father's household by a scarlet line in a window, is named in Hebrews 11 for faith and in James 2 for works, and is the great-great-grandmother of David. God's judgment fell on a city because of one man's hidden sin, and God's mercy spared a household because of one woman's open faith.
roots_summary: Hebrew ra'ah (H7200), to see, to look; ragal (H7270), to go on foot as a spy, to search out; neged (H5048), over against, in sight of.
roots_lines: Hebrew ra'ah (H7200) — to see, to look at, to survey; Joshua 2:1, 7:2.
Hebrew ragal (H7270) — to go about on foot, to spy out, to search; the verb behind to spy secretly.
Hebrew neged (H5048) — opposite, over against, in sight of; 2 Kings 2:7, stood to view afar off.
Hebrew cherem (H2764) — the devoted or accursed thing; what Achan took, and why Ai stood.
Hebrew tiqvah (H8615) — a cord, and also hope; Joshua 2:18, the scarlet line in Rahab's window.
usage: “Go view the land, even Jericho” — and they lodged with Rahab.
“The men went up and viewed Ai” — and the report was accurate and useless.
“Fifty men… stood to view afar off” — and two walked to the river.

pos: adj. (comparative of young; and in the Pastorals, a class within the church)
etymology: Comparative of young, Saxon geong. In Genesis the word marks God's repeated overturning of the rule of the firstborn; in the epistles it marks an order of respect and duty within the household of faith.
biblical_def: The word runs through Genesis as the signature of election. Rebekah is told before the twins are born, and before either had done good or evil: “Two nations are in thy womb… and the elder shall serve the younger” (Gen 25:23). Paul quotes exactly that verse in Romans 9 as the proof that God's purpose according to election stands, not of works but of Him that calleth. Jacob is called “her younger son” twice in the chapter where he steals the blessing (Gen 27:15, 42), and the same pattern runs through the book: Abel over Cain, Isaac over Ishmael, Ephraim over Manasseh, David over seven brothers. God does not honour the world's order of precedence, and He says so before the sons are born so that no one can mistake the reason. Laban's daughters give the plain domestic use — “the name of the elder was Leah, and the name of the younger was Rachel” (Gen 29:16) — and Jacob's seven years for “Rachel thy younger daughter” (Gen 29:18) ended in a substitution he had earned. The word's dark occurrence is Noah's: he “knew what his younger son had done unto him” (Gen 9:24). And in the New Testament it becomes an order of duty: rebuke not an elder, but intreat the younger men as brethren, and the younger women as sisters, with all purity.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines young as being in the first part of life or growth, not advanced in age; and younger as its comparative, of less age than another.
webster_full: YOUNG, a. Being in the first part of life or growth; as a young man; a young plant.
1. Ignorant; weak; or affected with the follies of youth.
YOUNGER, a. comp. Of less age than another; junior.
ELDER, a. Older; senior; having lived a longer time; born, produced or formed before something else.
scriptures: And the LORD said unto her, Two nations are in thy womb, and two manner of people shall be separated from thy bowels; and the one people shall be stronger than the other people; and the elder shall serve the younger.
And Laban had two daughters: the name of the elder was Leah, and the name of the younger was Rachel.

And these words of Esau her elder son were told to Rebekah: and she sent and called Jacob her younger son, and said unto him, Behold, thy brother Esau, as touching thee, doth comfort himself, purposing to kill thee.
Gen 9:24
And Noah awoke from his wine, and knew what his younger son had done unto him.
corruption_summary: Age-segregation has replaced the biblical order in which the younger learn from the elder and the elder are honoured by the younger.
corruption_paragraphs: The New Testament sets the generations in a working relationship rather than in separate rooms. Ye younger, submit yourselves unto the elder (1Pe 5:5); the aged women are to teach the young women to love their husbands and their children (Tit 2:3-5); Timothy is told to intreat the elder men as fathers and the younger as brethren (1Ti 5:1-2). The modern arrangement, in which every age has its own ministry, its own music and its own room, quietly removes the mechanism by which one generation transmits anything to the next. It produces a church in which the young are entertained by their peers and the old are stored, and it is not what the Pastorals describe.

The Genesis use guards against the opposite error, which is the sanctification of natural precedence. God repeatedly set aside the firstborn — the elder shall serve the younger, said before the twins were born, that the purpose of God according to election might stand, not of works, but of him that calleth. Order in the household of God is real and is to be honoured; it is never a claim on God. The last shall be first, and the first last, and no one has standing with Him by birth, seniority or precedence.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsa'ir (H6810), little, young, younger; bekor (H1060), firstborn; Greek neoteros (G3501), younger.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsa'ir (H6810) — little, insignificant, younger; Genesis 25:23, 29:16, and of Bethlehem in Micah 5:2, little among the thousands of Judah.
Hebrew qatan (H6996) — small, young; Genesis 9:24, Noah's younger son.
Hebrew bekor (H1060) — firstborn; the natural precedence God so often set aside.
Greek neoteros (G3501) — younger; 1 Timothy 5:1-2, 5:11, Titus 2:6, 1 Peter 5:5, Luke 15:12-13 (the younger son).
Greek ekloge (G1589) — election; Romans 9:11-12, where Genesis 25:23 is quoted to establish it.
usage: “The elder shall serve the younger” — said before the twins were born.
“The name of the younger was Rachel” — and seven years became fourteen.
“Knew what his younger son had done unto him” — the first drunkenness in Scripture.
